new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Wetar languages, Perai included (Uhak village list), word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; forms deviating from this are marked in the survey wordlist with an apostrophe before the stressed syllable, and in the c. 200-item Perai list only one form is so marked ('oinume 'where', initial/antepenultimate stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Exceptions are marked ad hoc with a preceding apostrophe in the wordlists; for Perai only 'oinume 'where' (item 151) carries it. (The clitic-induced stress shift with aspectual -e/-me, sec. 6.2 pp.115-116, is stated for Tugun only, not Perai.) Editor's note p.119: apparent monosyllables should be read as like-vowel sequences (e.g. /ron/ = /roon/), with stress still penultimate.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is a survey-level generalization over all five Wetar languages, applied to isolated citation forms in an elicited 210-word survey list (Uhak village, Perai); word-level stress, no phrase-level discussion. Not a Perai-specific phonological analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Hinton 2000's statement is a blanket generalization over the five Wetar languages (Perai, Aputai, Tugun, Ili'uun, Talur); the Perai data it applies to is the Uhak village wordlist (Perai is spoken in Uhak and Moning, NE Wetar). Perai = pera1257 / ISO wet; Hinton notes 79-80% lexical similarity with Aputai (aput1237), 'right at the threshold between language and dialect'. The same file and p.119 sentence already serve as deciding source for sibling audits tugu1245 and iliu1237.
